title: Deleuze and Guattari
tradition: Poststructuralism: the philosophy of difference and becoming
keyWorks: Deleuze, Spinoza: Practical Philosophy (1970, expanded ed. 1981)
Deleuze and Guattari, A Thousand Plateaus (1980)
Deleuze, “Postscript on the Societies of Control” (1990)
Deleuze and Guattari, What Is Philosophy? (1991)
summary: The philosopher Gilles Deleuze and the psychoanalyst Félix Guattari saw the world not as a collection of fixed things but as movement, encounters and transformations. What interests them is not “what you are” but “what you are capable of” and “what you are becoming.” The key words of this philosophy are “becoming,” “rhizome” (a network without a center), “desiring-production” and “affect.”
onEmotions: Following Spinoza, Deleuze understands “affect” as a passage: a change in our power of acting when we encounter other bodies, people, ideas, places. A joyful affect increases this power; a sad one decreases it. This is not a judgment of “good/bad” but a measure of strength. A feeling here is not your private property locked up inside, but an event between you and the world. And desire, according to Anti-Oedipus, is not a lack of something but a productive force that connects and builds. So the question to put to any feeling is this: what encounter brought it about, and what is it doing to your capacity to live?

anxiety.text: Anxiety is an understandable reaction to a world that doesn't let you stop. In “Postscript on the Societies of Control” Deleuze described a change of eras. In the disciplinary society Foucault wrote about, you moved from one enclosed place to another — school, army, factory — and each stage came to an end. In the society of control, Deleuze says, nothing is ever finished: continuous training, constant assessment, an endless “modulation,” like a dial that keeps being turned. From this angle one could say that anxiety is the feeling of an endlessly open file that has no last page. It is not your personal defect but the climate of the era. What helps is not always “calming down,” but noticing how few places in life allow you to put a full stop — and creating such places on purpose.
anxiety.practice: Choose one very small task and see it through to the end. Put a full stop at the end — literally, on paper — and notice the feeling.

fear.text: Fear is an ancient and very bodily feeling, and it doesn't make you weak. One of the chapters of A Thousand Plateaus opens with a simple scene: a child in the dark, gripped by fear, comforts himself by singing a little song. Deleuze and Guattari call this a “refrain” — a repeated motif that creates a small territory around us, an island of stability in the midst of chaos. Later, they say, one can step out of such a territory to meet the world. From this angle fear is not something to be crushed by willpower, but a signal that you need a small home of your own: a tune, a gesture, a familiar route, a phrase. The refrain doesn't cancel the danger, but it gives you a foothold from which the next step becomes possible.
fear.practice: What is your refrain — a song, a gesture, a phrase or a route that creates a sense of “my own place”? Use it now.

quote.text: A child in the dark, gripped with fear, comforts himself by singing under his breath.
quote.author: Gilles Deleuze and Félix Guattari
quote.source: A Thousand Plateaus (1980), plateau “1837: Of the Refrain”

sadness.text: Sadness is a real experience, and there is no need to be ashamed of it. Reading Spinoza, Deleuze describes sadness as an affect in which our power of acting decreases: we have met something — a person, a circumstance, a thought — that does not “agree” with us. This is not a verdict or a sin, but information about an encounter. At the same time, Deleuze pays close attention to how sadness is used: in his book on Spinoza he shows that those who want to dominate benefit from people sunk in “sad passions” — guilt, accusation, self-hatred. So sadness shouldn't be turned into self-blame: that only multiplies it. You can read it as a map — which connections are weakening you right now — and gently look for encounters that add even a little strength.
sadness.practice: Recall the last encounter — with a person, a place, an activity — after which you felt even a little lighter. Could you repeat something like it today?

grief.text: Grief is an immense experience, and it has no correct timeline. In The Logic of Sense, drawing on the ancient Stoics, Deleuze speaks of the “event” — what happens to us and what we did not choose. His ethical formula sounds unexpected: not to be unworthy of what happens to us. This is not a call to rejoice in a loss or to resign yourself to it. Rather, it means living through the event so that it does not make us smaller and harder, but becomes part of what we are becoming. From Deleuze's point of view one might add: the person you lost changed your capacity to feel, to see, to laugh, to care. These affects do not disappear with them — they go on living in you as your own capacities.
grief.practice: What capacity — to see, to joke, to care, to listen — did this bond leave in you? Write it down as something that goes on living.

quote.text: Either ethics makes no sense at all, or this is what it means and has nothing else to say: not to be unworthy of what happens to us.
quote.author: Gilles Deleuze
quote.source: The Logic of Sense (1969), Twenty-First Series of the Event

loneliness.text: Loneliness can be very painful, and longing for closeness is natural. Deleuze and Guattari did not see a person as a closed unit: each of us is an “assemblage,” a weave of connections with people, things, languages, places. In Dialogues Deleuze spoke of a “populated solitude”: we are deserts, but deserts populated by tribes, flora and fauna. From this angle one could say that loneliness is rarely absolute emptiness: it is populated by voices, books, memories, animals, smells, melodies. This doesn't cancel the pain of missing people close to you, nor does it replace them. But it can loosen a little the terrible feeling of total isolation: you are still part of many connections, and new encounters are possible precisely because you are open to them.
loneliness.practice: List who and what “populates” your solitude right now: voices, books, sounds, a plant on the windowsill, someone's words.

anger.text: Anger is a strong and legitimate feeling, and there is a lot of energy in it. Spinoza, whom Deleuze considered his main teacher, described anger as a sad passion: it is born of an encounter that diminishes us. But Deleuze and Guattari are not moralists; they don't say “anger is bad.” What interests them is where the intensity flows. In A Thousand Plateaus they speak of “lines of flight” — breakthroughs out of what is constricting and frozen — and at the same time warn that the same force can turn into pure destruction that creates nothing. From this angle one could say that anger is a charge that has not yet chosen its direction. It can become a new action, a boundary, creativity — or it can become bitterness. The choice of direction is largely in your hands.
anger.practice: Ask your anger: what does it want to create, not only destroy? Write down one possible “creative” direction.

shame.text: Shame burns, and many people know this feeling. Deleuze also spoke of another shame — “the shame of being a man” (Primo Levi's phrase): shame at what people do to one another, at the petty compromises and meannesses of the age. For him this was not a reason to hate oneself but one of the strongest pushes toward thought and creation. As for personal shame, Deleuze and Guattari help us see it through the concept of “faciality”: in A Thousand Plateaus the face is a machine that compares everyone against a norm and marks the deviations. Shame is burning under the gaze of such a “judge-face.” The way out, in their view, is not to put on the right face but “becoming”: a movement in which you are more than the features you are judged by.
shame.practice: For a minute, describe yourself not through qualities (“I am such-and-such”) but through what you are doing right now and what you are involved in.

quote.text: The shame of being a man — is there any better reason to write?
quote.author: Gilles Deleuze
quote.source: Essays Critical and Clinical (1993), “Literature and Life”

guilt.text: Guilt shows that how you act matters to you, and that is valuable. Deleuze and Guattari, however, looked very closely at how guilt works. In Anti-Oedipus they criticized psychoanalysis for reducing all the richness of desire to the family triangle “daddy–mommy–me” and for training people into endless debt. Deleuze, following Nietzsche, called such forces “reactive”: they turn life's energy against itself. And Spinoza, Deleuze's favorite philosopher, wrote that repentance is not a virtue: it adds a second sadness to the first. From this angle two things can be told apart: “I made a mistake and can put something right” — that is action; “I am bad forever” — that is a sadness that helps no one. Responsibility is possible without self-abasement.
guilt.practice: Rephrase the guilt as an action: “What I can do is this: …”. If it can't be put right — what will you take with you as a lesson?

envy.text: Envy is an unpleasant but entirely ordinary feeling. The main move of Anti-Oedipus is the idea that desire is not lack. Desire is production: it connects, builds, invents. The notion of desire as an eternal shortfall, according to Deleuze and Guattari, is largely created and organized by society — including the market, which benefits from our always lacking something. Envy lives precisely in the logic of lack: “she has it, I don't.” From this angle one could say that behind envy there often hides a living desiring-production — a desire to do, to try, to create — which for now is expressed as a desire to have. If you translate it from “having” into “doing,” envy turns into a hint about direction.
envy.practice: Translate the envy from “having” into “doing”: what activity, not what thing, did you see in the other person? What small part of it is open to you?

emptiness.text: Emptiness and apathy can be agonizing, and they are not your fault. Deleuze and Guattari speak of the “body without organs” — a strange expression they took from the poet Antonin Artaud. It is not about a body literally without organs, but about a state in which habitual, fixed functions and roles are lifted — a kind of zero point from which new movements can begin. At the same time, they insistently warn that such a state can turn out to be merely “emptied” if everything is destroyed at once. Their advice is caution and dosage. From this angle, apathy is like a moment when the old roles have switched off and the new has not yet arrived. Nothing needs to be broken or urgently rebuilt: what matters is keeping your supports while something new slowly gathers strength.
emptiness.practice: Name three small supports — food, sleep, a walk, one phone call — that you will keep today while the emptiness looks for a new form.

quote.text: You have to keep enough of the organism for it to reform each dawn.
quote.author: Gilles Deleuze and Félix Guattari
quote.source: A Thousand Plateaus (1980), plateau “How Do You Make Yourself a Body without Organs?”

confusion.text: Feeling lost is natural when life stops fitting into an understandable plan. Deleuze and Guattari contrast two images of thought. The “tree” — root, trunk, branches: there is a beginning, a hierarchy, a single right path. The “rhizome” — a rootstock, like couch grass or ginger: it has no center, any point can connect with any other, and growth goes in all directions. From this angle one could say that confusion often arises when we expect life to be a “tree,” while it is actually shaped like a rhizome. This is freeing: you don't have to know where it all began or how it will end. You can start from the middle — from the nearest connection, the nearest step sideways — and the path will be made of connections rather than of a plan drawn up in advance.
confusion.practice: Don't decide “where to, overall.” Find one nearest connection — a person, an activity, a book — and take one small step toward it.

quote.text: A rhizome has no beginning or end; it is always in the middle, between things.
quote.author: Gilles Deleuze and Félix Guattari

fatigue.text: Tiredness and burnout are not laziness but a sign that your strength really is running out. In the late essay “The Exhausted,” devoted to Beckett, Deleuze distinguishes two states. The tired person has exhausted realization: they no longer have the strength to do. The exhausted person has exhausted possibilities themselves: goals, plans, options for “what next” stop calling. Deleuze doesn't romanticize this state, but he doesn't see it only as failure either: when projects fall away, what remains is the possibility of simply seeing, hearing, being with an image, a sound, a space. From this angle one could say that burnout is not a verdict on your worth but a moment when the familiar machine of goals has stopped. You don't have to come up with new plans right now; you can briefly allow yourself to want nothing.
fatigue.practice: Allow yourself five minutes of planning nothing. Just notice one image around you — a patch of light, a sound, a shape — and stay with it.

boredom.text: Boredom is an honest signal that life has become too predictable. In Difference and Repetition Deleuze distinguishes two kinds of repetition. One is “bare,” mechanical: the same thing is reproduced without change. The other is alive, like a rhythm, a habit or the turning of the seasons: each time a small difference arises in it, and it is precisely this difference that makes repetition creative. From this angle one could say that boredom is the experience of a repetition in which we have stopped noticing differences. Desiring-production, for Deleuze and Guattari, is always looking for new connections; boredom is a sign that its flows have been blocked by a familiar pattern. You don't have to break your routine: sometimes it is enough to learn to see the difference within the repetition.
boredom.practice: In one habitual action — tea, your commute, washing your face — find a detail that is different today from yesterday.

joy.text: Joy is a beautiful feeling, and you don't need to earn it or be shy about it. For Spinoza and Deleuze, joy is a passage to a greater power of acting: you have met a body, a person or an idea that “agrees” with you, and your forces have combined. Deleuze calls Spinoza's philosophy an “ethics of joy”: not a code of prohibitions but the art of telling apart the encounters that strengthen us and building a life out of them. A favorite thought of Deleuze's, taken from Spinoza: we do not yet know what a body can do. Joy is a moment when this opens up a little. From this angle it is worth not only living through joy but also noticing its “composition”: what exactly met and combined — so that you can seek out such encounters again.
joy.practice: Write down the “recipe” for this joy: what met with what — people, place, time, action — for it to arise?

love.text: Love and tenderness are among the most alive of affects. Spinoza defined love as joy accompanied by the idea of an external cause. In Proust and Signs Deleuze adds a subtle thought: to love is to try to decipher the signs the beloved gives off, to “unfold” the unknown worlds enfolded within them. The beloved is not an object but a whole world into which we are only partly admitted. And in A Thousand Plateaus love can be understood as “becoming”: two people don't merge into one or copy each other, but each begins to become something new thanks to the other. From this angle tenderness is not possession but a movement in which you both change — and it is fine that the other can never be fully understood.
love.practice: What “world” of the other — a habit, a pet word, a taste, a way of looking — has unfolded in you thanks to this love?

gratitude.text: Gratitude is a joyful affect, and there is great strength in it. Spinoza defined it as the desire to repay with love someone who has done us good out of love. From Deleuze and Guattari's point of view one might add: gratitude is knowledge of what we are assembled from. For them a person is not a solitary “I” but an assemblage of many influences: people, books, places, languages, chance encounters. They themselves stressed that their books were written not by two authors but by a whole multitude of voices that passed through them. Gratitude, then, is not a polite duty but a way of seeing your life as a rhizome of connections, where every thread has given you something. This is joyful, and it also frees you a little from the illusion that you have to carry everything alone.
gratitude.practice: Draw a “map of your assemblage”: five people, things or places that today's day is assembled from. Which of them are you grateful to?

quote.text: The two of us wrote Anti-Oedipus together. Since each of us was several, there was already quite a crowd.
quote.author: Gilles Deleuze and Félix Guattari

hope.text: Hope is an understandable and necessary feeling, especially in hard times. But Deleuze looks at it after Spinoza, for whom hope and fear are two sides of one thing: there is no hope without fear and no fear without hope, since both live by expecting what does not depend on us. Deleuze proposes a shift: not to give up hope, but to turn waiting into action. In “Postscript on the Societies of Control” he writes that there is no need to fear or to hope — what we need is to look for new weapons. “Weapons” here means new ways of acting, connections, practices. From this angle hope becomes not something you wait for but something you do: a small step that is already changing your capacity to live.
hope.practice: What one “new weapon” — a small action, a connection, a habit — can you find today within your strength?

quote.text: There is no need to fear or hope, but only to look for new weapons.
quote.author: Gilles Deleuze

nostalgia.text: Nostalgia is a warm longing for a place, a time, people, and it speaks of what was dear to you. Deleuze and Guattari call the loss of a familiar territory “deterritorialization,” and the gaining of a new one “reterritorialization.” They stress that this is a continuous process: we are constantly losing some footholds and gathering others. From this angle nostalgia is the feeling of a lost territory. Moreover, Deleuze, drawing on Bergson, said that the past does not disappear: it coexists with the present as the “virtual” — a living reserve that can reappear in new forms. One could say that nostalgia is a touch of this reserve. The past cannot be brought back whole, but seeds can be carried from it into a new territory.
nostalgia.practice: What from that lost “territory” — a taste, a habit, a song, a way of spending the evening — could you carry into your life today, like seeds?

craving.text: A craving — a sharp “I want it right now” — can be almost unbearable, and it doesn't make you weak or bad. Deleuze and Guattari understand desire not as lack but as a force that connects: the body with people, places, activities. From their point of view one could say that a craving is desire narrowed down to one single connection and insisting that there are no others. They wrote about drugs critically: such experiments, in their words, fail again and again; the “line of flight” (a way out of what confines you) turns into a line of destruction, and the person falls back into what they wanted to escape. Their question is sober: how do you find aliveness and a way out of confinement without a substance? A wave of craving rises and falls; while it passes, you can look for other connections, however small.
craving.practice: When a wave of craving rises, name one other connection available right now: a glass of water, a window, a sound, a person's voice. Notice how the wave changes while you do this.

addiction.text: Addiction is a long cycle in which life gradually becomes organized around one thing, and it is hard to get out of. It is not a moral failure. Deleuze and Guattari spoke of the “body without organs” — a state in which habitual roles are lifted and room opens up for something new. But in A Thousand Plateaus they warn directly: in the drug addict such a body turns out to be “emptied,” glazed — instead of an opening, the result is a frozen cycle. In the article “Two Questions on Drugs” (1978) Deleuze also acknowledged that the drug promises a line of flight but leads to a line of destruction. Their sober conclusion is that aliveness has to be sought otherwise; they recalled Henry Miller, who dreamed of getting drunk on pure water. Guattari worked all his life at the La Borde clinic and believed in the collective: one gets out of a solitary cycle through new connections with people, places, activities.
addiction.practice: Draw your “map of connections”: people, places, pursuits that once gave you strength. If you like, one of the points could be a mutual-help group or a person who knows this path from the inside.

hangover.text: A hangover is heaviness in the body and also morning anxiety, shame, gaps in memory. All of this is tormenting, and you deserve gentleness, not a verdict. In The Logic of Sense Deleuze recalls Fitzgerald's essay “The Crack-Up” — about a crack that silently runs through the life of a man who drinks. Deleuze does not admire this; he asks whether it is possible to speak of such experiences without paying for them with one's health, and admits how easy it is to reason about someone else's destruction from the outside. From the standpoint of Deleuze and Spinoza one could say that in the morning the body honestly reports a “sad affect” — a decrease in the power of acting. This is not a judgment on you but a report on the state of your strength. You can take note of it without turning it into a verdict, and let your body recover.
hangover.practice: Without going over last night minute by minute, write down only one thing: what your body needs now — water, food, quiet, sleep — and give it that.

euphoria.text: A burst of euphoria is a sudden high when everything seems possible. It is a real experience, and there is no need to be ashamed of it or to snuff it out immediately. Deleuze, following Spinoza, distinguishes among joys. Spinoza distinguished “titillation” (titillatio) — a pleasure that seizes one part of us and can therefore become excessive — from “cheerfulness” (hilaritas), a joy in which the whole body takes part. And in A Thousand Plateaus Deleuze and Guattari advise leaving familiar frameworks not with a sledgehammer but with a “very fine file” — carefully, dosing the intensity. From this angle one could say: euphoria is best neither revved up nor suppressed, but distributed — let it spread through your whole body, across different activities and people, so that it doesn't burn out at a single point.
euphoria.practice: Let the joy “spread through your body”: take a walk, stretch, say a warm word to someone. Write down one idea from this high so that it will still be waiting for you tomorrow.

crash.text: A sharp drop after a high — a celebration, a success, a substance — can be very hard: as if the lights had been switched off. This is an understandable reaction, not proof that the joy was “not real.” Spinoza and Deleuze describe affect as a passage: the power of acting grows or diminishes. From this angle one could say that the comedown is a passage downward, a “sad affect,” not a new truth about you. Deleuze and Guattari noted that every exit from the familiar is accompanied by “reterritorialization” — a return to old territory — and sometimes this feels like a fall. You don't need to urgently look for a new peak in order to get out. Their advice from A Thousand Plateaus is caution and keeping your supports: a little familiar order helps the body get through the slump and regain strength.
crash.practice: Mark on paper where you are right now on an imaginary wave: not “I've failed” but “I'm in a dip.” Choose one support for the next hour.

panic.text: Panic is one of the most frightening experiences: your heart pounds, you can't get enough air, it seems something irreparable is about to happen. You really are scared, and this needs to be acknowledged. Deleuze and Guattari end What Is Philosophy? with a discussion of chaos: thoughts and sensations can race at infinite speed without time to take shape, and nothing is more distressing than a thought that escapes itself. That is why, they say, we ask for very little — only a little order. From this angle one could say that in panic what you need is not an answer to every question but the simplest form: the rhythm of breathing, counting, a sense of support — like a refrain, the little song with which a child draws a safe circle in the dark. A wave of panic usually peaks and subsides within a few minutes; rhythm helps you wait it out.
panic.practice: Put your feet on the floor and breathe so that the exhale is longer than the inhale: in for a count of four, out for six. Repeat the rhythm like a song, and silently name the objects around you.

quote.text: We require just a little order to protect us from chaos.
quote.author: Gilles Deleuze and Félix Guattari
quote.source: What Is Philosophy? (1991), conclusion “From Chaos to the Brain”

dread.text: Existential dread — “what is it all for,” finitude, the abyss — is one of the heaviest feelings, and many thoughtful people have lived through it. Deleuze doesn't answer it with a comforting tale of a “higher meaning.” His philosophy is a philosophy of “immanence”: meaning is not hidden above the world or after it; it arises here, in encounters and deeds themselves. In Spinoza: Practical Philosophy Deleuze writes with admiration of how Spinoza exposed everything that devalues life, and recalls his thought: wisdom is a meditation not on death but on life. From this angle the abyss is not an answer but a question that turns you toward life: what encounters, here and now, make it stronger? The answers can be very simple — a taste, a face, a task.
dread.practice: Write down three things from today that added even a little life to you — not great things, just real ones: a smell, a voice, light.

fomo.text: The fear of missing out — the sense that real life is happening somewhere else — is something very many people feel today. In Anti-Oedipus Deleuze and Guattari argue with the familiar idea of desire as lack. They write that lack is not natural: it is created, planned and organized — including by the market and consumer society. From this angle one could say that the fear of missing out is largely a manufactured feeling: the feed is designed so that you are always missing something. This is not your flaw. And desire, for Deleuze, is a productive force: it builds “assemblages,” living combinations of people, things and activities, here, out of what is near. The question is not “where is everyone?” but “what can I connect and build where I am?”
fomo.practice: Describe your “assemblage” for today in one sentence: which person, place or activity near you together make up your life today.

sleepless.text: Insomnia and thoughts at three in the morning are exhausting: at night everything seems bigger and scarier. This is not weakness — the nighttime mind works differently. Deleuze and Guattari distinguished the “tree” from the “rhizome.” The tree thinks hierarchically: from root to branches, from cause to conclusion. The rhizome is a network without a center, where any point can connect with any other. From this angle one could say that night thoughts are a rhizome that won't stop: one worry hooks onto another, and there is no trunk to climb down to a clear conclusion. Solutions aren't found in such a network, and that's normal. What helps is not thinking everything through to the end, but gently acknowledging: this is the night network, not the daytime truth. In the morning the connections will rearrange themselves.
sleepless.practice: Write down the main knots of the night network — three or four words, no conclusions — and set the sheet aside until morning. Tell yourself: “The network is written down; I don't need to hold it in my head.”

betrayal.text: Betrayal wounds deeply: what collapses is not only the bond with a person but also trust in your own judgment. Your pain is legitimate. Deleuze and Guattari describe relationships as “assemblages” (agencements) — living connections of people, habits, promises, places. An assemblage is not eternal: people leave it along “lines of flight.” In Dialogues with Claire Parnet Deleuze remarks that there is something of betrayal in every line of flight. This is not an excuse for the one who betrayed you, nor a demand that you understand them. But it lifts one weight from you: betrayal speaks of an assemblage coming apart and of someone else's movement, not of your having been foolish to trust. Trust is a capacity, not a mistake. In time it can be invested in new, more reliable connections.
betrayal.practice: Name one person or one endeavor you continue to trust. Note: your capacity to trust has stayed with you.

jealousy.text: Jealousy is tormenting: it turns the person you love into a riddle and you into an investigator. Almost everyone who has loved knows this feeling. In Proust and Signs Deleuze takes jealousy seriously. To love, in his view, is to decipher the signs the other gives off, and jealousy is the extreme form of this deciphering: every word, gesture, late arrival becomes a hieroglyph pointing to an unknown world from which you are excluded. Deleuze even writes that jealousy is deeper than love and contains its truth: the other always carries within them worlds that do not belong to us. From this angle jealousy is not a sign that you are somehow “wrong” but a painful encounter with the fact that the other cannot become your property. That is how love for a living person works.
jealousy.practice: Divide a sheet of paper into two columns: “signs I see” and “stories I add to them.” Notice how much room the second one takes up.

resentment.text: An old grudge is heavy: you carry it with you, and it doesn't let go even when you want it to. In Nietzsche and Philosophy Deleuze examines in detail Nietzsche's concept of “ressentiment” — hidden, festering resentment. His explanation is not moral but almost physiological: in the person of ressentiment the trace of the wound is never erased; the memory of it takes over all of consciousness and crowds out the capacity to act anew. Following Nietzsche, Deleuze calls active forgetting the healthy force — not denying the hurt, but being able to make it stop taking up all the room. From this angle your grudge speaks of a real wound. The question is not whether to forgive immediately, but how to regain your capacity to act — so that the old trace lives in you but doesn't govern you.
resentment.practice: Write down one thing the grudge is keeping you from doing. Today, do a tiny part of it — not for the sake of forgiveness, but for the sake of your own strength.

heartbreak.text: A breakup can feel as if the ground has been knocked out from under your feet, and that feeling is legitimate. Deleuze and Guattari describe life through “territories” — not only places but also habits, rhythms, shared jokes, smells that make the world your own. A couple is a territory too. A breakup is a “deterritorialization”: the territory falls apart, and you find yourself outside your familiar coordinates. But in their thinking, deterritorialization always goes hand in hand with “reterritorialization”: a new territory takes shape — not at once and not according to a blueprint. From this angle one could say that a broken heart is not the end of the story but a painful interval between territories. There is no need to rush the new one: it grows out of small things — a new route, a new song, rearranged furniture.
heartbreak.practice: Choose one small thing that will make your space a little bit your own again: a different order on a shelf, a new mug, another way home.

impostor.text: The feeling that you are about to be found out is familiar to many intelligent people, and it doesn't prove that you are where you are by accident. Deleuze, one of the boldest philosophers of the century, admitted in the preface to Difference and Repetition that one can only write at the frontier of one's knowledge — where it passes over into ignorance. That, he says, is exactly where you find something to say. Thought, for Deleuze, begins not with certainty but with a problem — with what forces us to think. From Deleuze's point of view one could say that the “impostor” is someone honestly standing at the edge of their skill, in the process of “becoming.” No one arrives in their place ready-made. The feeling of not being ready is a sign that you are still learning, not that you are a fraud.
impostor.practice: Finish the sentence: “I am at the frontier of my knowledge when it comes to…” Notice that this describes a path, not an exposure.

quote.text: How else can one write but of those things which one doesn't know, or knows badly?
quote.author: Gilles Deleuze

self_hatred.text: Self-hatred and the voice of the inner critic are tormenting, and that voice does not tell the truth about you. In Spinoza: Practical Philosophy Deleuze takes up one of Spinoza's most important ideas: the “sad passions” — guilt, hatred, contempt for oneself — diminish our power of acting. And, according to Deleuze, those who want to dominate have a stake in them: the tyrant and the priest need people who are sad about themselves. From this angle one could say that the inner critic is not a wise judge but the internalized voice of such power, speaking in your voice. Spinoza and Deleuze don't suggest fighting yourself even harder. They suggest seeking encounters that increase your strength even a little — and noticing how the critic quiets down as a result.
self_hatred.practice: Write down one phrase of the critic and ask: “Whose voice is this? Who benefits from my thinking this way?” Then name one thing that added to your strength today, however small.

helplessness.text: Helplessness — the feeling that nothing depends on you — is heavy and often very real: there are circumstances that are beyond one person's power. Following Spinoza, Deleuze asks, “what can a body do?” — and stresses that we don't know in advance. Power here is not omnipotence but a concrete capacity to act, which changes with encounters. Deleuze and Guattari also speak of “micropolitics”: besides big decisions, there are countless small, “molecular” movements — a gesture, a conversation, a small change in the rhythm of the day. From this angle one could say: if the big thing can't be changed, that doesn't mean your power equals zero. It has simply moved to a finer level, where it is easy to overlook.
helplessness.practice: Draw two circles: a large one — “what I can't change,” and a small one — “what I can do in the next hour.” Write at least one action in the small one.

procrastination.text: “I can't get started” is a very familiar and draining state, and it doesn't mean laziness. In his book on the painter Francis Bacon (The Logic of Sensation), Deleuze makes an unexpected observation: the blank canvas is not actually empty. It is filled in advance with clichés — ready-made images, expectations, the way things are “supposed” to be. The painter first has to battle this invisible load. From this angle one could say that procrastination is not emptiness but overfullness: in front of you stand other people's models and a picture of the ideal result. And Deleuze and Guattari advise starting not from the beginning but “from the middle,” the way a rhizome grows — not with the first sentence, but from any place where you can get in.
procrastination.practice: Start from the middle: for five minutes, work on any piece of the task except the first — a paragraph from the middle, one cell of a spreadsheet.

uprooted.text: Being cut off from home — after emigration or a move — can be very painful: you lose a language, habits, people, the very ground under you. This is a real loss. Deleuze and Guattari call it “deterritorialization” — leaving a familiar territory. In their work the word sounds neither like a tragedy nor like a celebration: this is how everything alive lives. Their “nomad” is not someone who travels a lot, but someone who knows how to inhabit space while moving. And in their book Kafka they describe “minor literature” — the writing of a minority in the language of the majority, as with Kafka, a Prague Jew who wrote in German. Such speech, in their view, is not poorer but sharper and more inventive. From this angle one could say that your accent and your “incorrectness” are not a defect but a form of creativity.
uprooted.practice: Find one small “refrain” — a song, a dish, a morning ritual — that links your former home with your present one, and repeat it today.

overload.text: Overload — an endless feed, notifications, a noise in which it's impossible to collect yourself — wears out a great many people, and it is not your personal inability. Deleuze wrote about “societies of control,” where power acts through continuous flows of information. In one of the interviews collected in Negotiations he remarked that the trouble is not that people are prevented from expressing themselves but that they are swamped with pointless words — what is needed are gaps of solitude and silence in which one might eventually find something to say. In a conversation with Antonio Negri he proposed creating “vacuoles of noncommunication” — a kind of circuit breakers. From this angle your overload is a normal response to an environment designed to keep you always connected. And a vacuole can be very small.
overload.practice: Set up one “vacuole” for ten minutes: phone in another room, nothing incoming. Notice what thought appears once the noise dies down.

quote.text: The key thing may be to create vacuoles of noncommunication, circuit breakers, so we can elude control.
quote.author: Gilles Deleuze
quote.source: Negotiations (1990), conversation with Antonio Negri, “Control and Becoming”

unreality.text: The feeling that everything around you, or you yourself, is somehow not real can be very strange and frightening. It deserves gentle treatment. Deleuze has an important distinction between the “virtual” and the “actual.” The virtual is neither “unreal” nor computer-generated: it is real but not yet unfolded possibilities, like memory or a reserve of strength, which are not visible but exist. From this angle one could say that in moments of unreality the actual world seems to recede and lose its density. In Cinema 2 Deleuze wrote that the link between a person and the world can be broken, and that restoring belief in this world, in this life, is a difficult but essential task. Such a return begins not with reasoning but with simple contact: weight, warmth, sound.
unreality.practice: Take some object in your hand and name three of its qualities: weight, temperature, texture. This is your small link with the world right now.

awe.text: Awe before something vast or beautiful — mountains, the sea, music, the night sky — is a rare and precious feeling. You can simply savor it. In What Is Philosophy? Deleuze and Guattari say that art creates “percepts” and “affects” — sensations that live on their own, independently of whoever experiences them. They cite Cézanne: man is absent from the landscape, yet entirely within it. From this angle awe is a moment when you stop being the center and become part of something greater; in A Thousand Plateaus this is called “becoming-world.” It is not a diminishing but an expansion: your body turns out to be able to hold more than usual.
awe.practice: Stay for a minute with whatever filled you with awe, and try to describe it without once saying “I”: only mountains, light, sound.

relief.text: Relief — when something lets go and you can finally breathe out — deserves to be noticed and lived. Following Spinoza, Deleuze understands affect as a passage: not a state but a movement from lesser power to greater, or the reverse. Relief is an almost pure example of such a passage. A body clenched with tension regains its capacity to move, think, rejoice; the world opens up again. From this angle relief is not merely the absence of something bad but a joyful affect, an increase in strength. Deleuze called Spinoza's ethics an “ethology” — the study of what strengthens and what weakens a particular body. Relief is an excellent teacher of such ethology: it shows exactly what was pressing on you and what helped.
relief.practice: Notice in your body where exactly it let go: shoulders, belly, breath. Write down what helped — as the first line of your own small “ethology.”

calm.text: Peace and tranquility are not emptiness or laziness but a special, full state. It is good simply to be in it. Deleuze and Guattari took the word “plateau” for A Thousand Plateaus from the anthropologist Gregory Bateson. Studying Balinese culture, Bateson described a “plateau” — a steady region of intensity that doesn't strive toward a culmination, a peak and a discharge. Deleuze and Guattari set the plateau against the habit of pushing everything to a climax and a crash. From this angle calm is not “nothing happening” but a plateau: an even, living intensity that doesn't need an explosion to be real. It doesn't need to be turned into productivity or accounted for.
calm.practice: Sit for a minute, noticing the evenness of this state: where in your body it is calm, what rhythm your breathing has. Add nothing — just stay on the plateau.

inspiration.text: Inspiration — when thoughts and images start coming on their own — is one of the most joyful states. In the interview “Mediators” (from the collection Negotiations) Deleuze says that creation is impossible without “mediators” — people, things, books, landscapes through which thought comes to us. Without them, he says, there is no work: even alone, we work with someone. And in What Is Philosophy? creation is described as making something new — concepts, sensations — out of an encounter with chaos. From this angle inspiration is not the gift of a solitary genius but a fortunate encounter, an “assemblage.” It doesn't need to be held on to by force: it is enough to notice who and what your mediators are right now, and to give them room.
inspiration.practice: Write down three “mediators” of this inspiration — a person, a thing, a place — and one idea while it's still hot.

schadenfreude.text: Schadenfreude is awkward to admit, but it is very human and says little about who you are. Following Spinoza, Deleuze distinguished among joys. There is a joy that increases our power of acting — when we create, meet, grow. And there is a strange “joy” that feeds on someone else's sadness. Spinoza observed that joy at the misfortune of someone we don't love is never free of an admixture of sadness: it gives no real strength. In Nietzsche and Philosophy Deleuze called such forces “reactive”: they don't create, they only respond to another. From this angle one could say: schadenfreude often signals a wound or powerlessness of your own. There is no need to be ashamed of it — better to ask what real joy you are lacking right now.
schadenfreude.practice: Ask yourself: what joy of my own, a creative one, am I lacking right now? Write down one small one that is available as soon as today.

contempt.text: Contempt can feel like strength: I am above this, I can see how worthless the other is. In Nietzsche and Philosophy Deleuze distinguished active and reactive forces. An active force affirms and creates; a reactive force defines itself through negating another: “they are bad — therefore I am good.” Nietzsche called the root of this outlook “ressentiment.” From this angle one could say: contempt is often a hidden reactive force that keeps you tied to the person you despise. You spend your energy on them rather than on your own life. This doesn't make you a bad person: reactive forces are in everyone. But you can ask what your contempt is protecting — and what you could affirm yourself, without comparison.
contempt.practice: Write down one thing you value without mentioning the person you despise. A pure affirmation, with no “unlike them.”

disgust.text: Disgust is a very bodily feeling, and it often knows something important. Deleuze loved Spinoza's idea, from his letters on evil, that poison is not evil “in general” but a bad encounter — a body that does not agree with ours and destroys it. Spinoza even explained Adam's forbidden apple as something like a poison. For Spinoza and Deleuze there is no “good and evil” as such, but good and bad encounters. From this angle one could say: disgust at a situation or at people is the body's signal of a bad encounter, of something here that diminishes your strength. It is not a moral verdict on the other. Disgust at yourself is a special case: it helps to ask whose gaze, whose yardstick has poisoned your encounter with yourself.
disgust.practice: Ask your disgust: what exactly here is diminishing my strength? Name it in one word.

revenge.text: The wish for revenge is a natural response to pain that has been inflicted, and there is no need to be ashamed of it. Following Nietzsche, Deleuze described “ressentiment” — a state in which the wound doesn't heal but is relived again and again, and the person keeps answering it in their mind with retribution. For Deleuze the trouble with ressentiment is that it ties us to the one who hurt us: life starts to revolve around them. Nietzsche spoke of “active forgetting” — the ability not to keep an old wound constantly in mind, so as to make room for the new. From this angle one could say: you don't have to forgive or pretend nothing happened. But you can notice that revenge keeps you inside someone else's story — and ask where you yourself want to go.
revenge.practice: Draw two arrows: one toward the person who hurt you, the other toward what you would like to do for yourself. By the second, write down one thing to do this week.

anger_at_loved.text: Anger at those close to us is a frequent and painful part of closeness, one we are often ashamed of afterward. In Anti-Oedipus Deleuze and Guattari argued against the habit of explaining everything through the “daddy–mommy–me” triangle. They believed our feelings are bound up not only with the family drama but with a multitude of forces: fatigue, work, money, cramped space, lack of time. From this angle one could say: anger at a loved one is often not caused by them alone. Much of what presses on you gathers in it, and the loved one simply happened to be nearby, at the point of encounter. Understanding this doesn't cancel responsibility for your words, but it removes excess guilt and drama. You can ask: what else, besides this person, is feeding my anger?
anger_at_loved.practice: When the anger subsides, list three things besides the person close to you that were pressing on you today.

ambivalence.text: Loving and not being able to stand the same person is a very common, if painful, state. Deleuze and Guattari disliked “either–or” questions. In A Thousand Plateaus they set against the tree, which rests on the verb “to be,” the rhizome, whose fabric is the conjunction “and… and… and….” From this angle one could say: your relationship is not a single feeling but many affects arising in different encounters. In one situation this person increases your power to live; in another, they decrease it. There is no need to work out which feeling is the “real” one. It is more useful to notice which encounters with them are joyful and which are sad. This doesn't destroy love; it makes it clearer and more alive.
ambivalence.practice: Write down: “I feel good with you when… And it's hard for me when…” Leave both sentences side by side.

guilty_relief.text: Relief after a hard ending — a breakup, the end of a loved one's long illness — often comes with shame. This is understandable, and it doesn't cancel love. Following Spinoza, Deleuze understood affect as a passage — a change in your capacity to live and act. From this angle one could say: relief is an affect marking the end of a long tension that was constricting your life. It says nothing about whether you loved; it says how much strength went into holding on. Love and relief are not at odds: they are different lines running at the same time. Deleuze would not judge this affect — he would ask what might now become possible again in your life.
guilty_relief.practice: Notice where in your body things have become a little freer. Stay with it, without rushing to judge yourself for it.

indifference.text: Sometimes you are untouched by what “should” move you, and that is frightening. Following Spinoza, Deleuze understood affects as changes in strength arising in encounters. In “Postscript on the Societies of Control” he described a world where we are continuously plugged into flows of information and demands. From this angle one could say: indifference doesn't necessarily mean a cold heart. When there are too many encounters and too much news, the capacity to respond can be temporarily dulled — as a defense. It is not a verdict. Deleuze spoke of “vacuoles of noncommunication” — pauses in which one can slip away from the flows. Perhaps your sensitivity needs such a pause. Or perhaps this particular encounter simply isn't yours — and that's normal too.
indifference.practice: Give yourself ten minutes without news or screens. Then ask: what do I have a living response to — even something small?

escape.text: Deleuze and Guattari would take the wish to drop everything — a job, a city, a role — seriously. They spoke of “lines of flight” — paths by which life breaks out of frozen forms. For them flight is not cowardice but a creative movement, a “deterritorialization” — going beyond the bounds of a familiar territory. But they also warned that escape by itself does not guarantee freedom. You can leave and build the same cage in a new place — “reterritorialize” onto the old. From this angle one could say: it is worth asking not only what you are running from, but also where your line leads. Sometimes the line of flight runs right here — through a new activity, a new connection, a different rhythm of life.
escape.practice: Draw your “line of flight”: from where — to where. Mark on it one small step that is possible right now.

quote.text: Never believe that a smooth space will suffice to save us.
quote.author: Gilles Deleuze and Félix Guattari
quote.source: A Thousand Plateaus (1980), plateau “1440: The Smooth and the Striated”

forbidden_attraction.text: Attraction to an unavailable or “wrong” person is disorienting, and there is nothing shameful in it. Deleuze and Guattari insisted: desire is not lack but production. Deleuze explained in the televised interview L'Abécédaire that we never desire simply someone or something; we desire an ensemble — a whole landscape, a world that opens up through a person. From this angle one could say: a forbidden attraction may point not so much to the person themselves as to the world glimpsed through them — another life, freedom, aliveness, attention. Asking yourself what “ensemble” you desire means understanding your desire better, without passing a verdict on yourself and without rushing to conclusions.
forbidden_attraction.practice: Describe not the person but the world they seem to open up: a place, a mood, a rhythm. What of this could you let more of into your own life?

social_anxiety.text: Fear of people and of being judged can freeze you: your voice trembles, your words get tangled. Deleuze wrote an essay, “He Stuttered,” in which stammering becomes not a flaw but a creative force: great writers, he says, make language itself “stutter,” making it foreign to itself. From this angle one could say: your awkwardness is not a failure to meet a norm of smooth speech but your own particular rhythm. Following Spinoza, Deleuze suggested asking not “what am I like in others' eyes?” but “what am I capable of in this encounter?” An encounter is not an exam but an event between people in which something can be born. Focusing on the task or the topic of conversation often weakens the gaze of the imaginary judge.
social_anxiety.practice: In your next conversation, focus on one thing: what interesting thing is the other person saying. Notice how the tension changes.

uncertainty.text: Uncertainty is heavy: you want to know what will happen, and you don't. Deleuze and Guattari wrote that thought and life are constantly dealing with chaos, and we need at least a little order to protect ourselves from it. But they did not see the task as eliminating the unknown. Their image is the “rhizome”: a network without a center that grows in different directions, finding new connections. A rhizome has no single plan, and yet it is hardy. From this angle one could say: uncertainty is not only a threat but also a space in which something new can appear. You don't need to see the whole map to take the next step. It is enough to find one living connection here and now.
uncertainty.practice: Instead of a plan for everything, write down one connection or one activity that supports you right now. Lean on it today.

waiting.text: Waiting — for an answer, results, news — drags on painfully, as if life had been put on pause. In Bergsonism Deleuze examines Henri Bergson's famous example: if you want to make a glass of sugar water, you have to wait for the sugar to dissolve. This waiting cannot be hurried — and it is precisely in it that Bergson saw real time, “duration”: time that is not measured but lived. Deleuze showed that duration is not an empty slicing into minutes but living change. From this angle one could say: while you wait, time is not empty. The sugar is dissolving — and something is changing in you too. You can stop counting the minutes and notice what is happening now.
waiting.practice: Pour some tea and watch the sugar dissolve or the cup cool. For a minute, simply be in this time.

regret.text: Regret over what you did or didn't do can come back again and again. Deleuze wrote about the “event”: what happened cannot be reduced to bare facts; it has a sense, and we can take it on in different ways. In The Logic of Sense, following the Stoics, he spoke of becoming worthy of what happens to us — without hating the past and without denying it. Nietzsche, whom Deleuze read very closely, called a similar attitude “amor fati” — love of fate. From this angle one could say: you don't have to approve of your mistakes, but you can stop waging war on what has already happened. Then the past becomes material for what you do next, rather than a chain pulling you back.
regret.practice: Write one sentence about what you regret: “This happened, and now I can…” — and finish it.

longing.text: Longing for a particular person hurts in a special way: it is exactly them you are missing. In Proust and Signs Deleuze wrote that a beloved person is a whole world enfolded within them: gestures, intonations, places we knew only through them. From this angle one could say: in longing, what has closed is not only the person but the whole world they opened up for you — which is why it is so vast. But Deleuze also showed something else: signs go on living in memory and can unexpectedly unfold again, like the taste of the madeleine that gave Proust back a whole town of his childhood. Longing is a sign that this world has entered you and remains part of you, even when the person is not near.
longing.practice: Recall one “sign” of this person — a smell, a melody, a pet word. Let it unfold: what world does it bring with it?

world_pain.text: Pain for the world — from wars, injustice, grim news — can be almost unbearable. It is a sign that you are open to the world. Following Primo Levi, Deleuze spoke of “the shame of being a man” — a feeling that arises at the sight of what people do to one another. But for Deleuze this feeling is not a reason for despair but one of the strongest pushes toward thought and creation. He said that to create is to resist: a book, a relationship, a community, a small gesture of care — these are already an answer. From this angle one could say: you don't have to carry the whole weight of the world alone. But out of this pain something alive can grow that increases the power to live — yours and others'.
world_pain.practice: Do one small creative thing today — for yourself or for others: write, cook, help. Let it be your answer.

rejection.text: Rejection hurts: it feels as if you have been assessed and found unnecessary. Deleuze and Guattari contrasted two images of life — the “tree” and the “rhizome.” A tree has one root: cut it and the tree falls. A rhizome is a network like mycelium or the rootstock of grass; in A Thousand Plateaus they wrote that it can be broken at any point, but it will start up again on its old lines or on new ones. From this angle one could say: rejection feels like a blow to the “root” if all your worth rests on a single connection or a single “yes.” But life is more like a rhizome: you have many lines — people, activities, interests, places. One line has snapped, and that hurts. But the network keeps growing.
rejection.practice: Draw your “rhizome”: five or six lines of connections and activities in your life. Mark which of them could grow a little stronger right now.

abandonment.text: The fear of being abandoned can run very deep, especially if you have been left before. Deleuze and Guattari argued against the familiar idea that desire is a lack, a void that only another person can fill. Such a picture makes us hostages: if the person leaves, we will be left “incomplete.” For them desire is the production of connections, and each person is not a half but a “multiplicity,” a network of relations with people, activities, places. From this angle one could say: your fear is understandable, especially if past experience was painful. But your life does not hang on a single thread. You can gently notice and strengthen other connections — not instead of the person close to you, but alongside them.
abandonment.practice: List the people, activities and places that support you besides the person closest to you. Choose one connection and give it some time this week.

unrequited.text: Unrequited love is a pain full of silence. In Proust and Signs Deleuze noted that the beloved always gives off signs of worlds we are not let into: they have a life we are not part of. In Proust, the torments of love are the painful deciphering of signs not addressed to us. But Deleuze showed something else too: this deciphering is an “apprenticeship.” Through the suffering of love we learn something about signs, about time, about ourselves. From this angle one could say: your love is not in vain, even if there is no answer. It opened a whole world to you and taught you to see it. That remains yours, and no one can take it away.
unrequited.practice: Write down: what has this love taught me? What do I see now that I didn't see before?

humiliation.text: Humiliation is one of the deepest wounds: someone tried to make you smaller. Following Spinoza, Deleuze believed that power often rests on “sad passions” — fear, shame, a sense of one's own worthlessness. In Spinoza: Practical Philosophy he wrote that the tyrant needs sad souls in order to rule. From this angle one could say: humiliation is a technique that seeks to diminish your power of acting. But it is something done to you, not the truth about you. The best response, for Spinoza and Deleuze, is not humiliation in return but a return of joyful affects — of everything that again increases your power to live. Every small joy here is already resistance.
humiliation.practice: Do one thing today that adds to your strength: a walk, a call to a friend, a favorite activity. Notice how you feel afterward.

body_shame.text: Dissatisfaction with your body can be a constant background: the mirror, photos, glances. This is a very common feeling. Deleuze loved to repeat Spinoza's thought: we do not even know what a body can do. For Spinoza and Deleuze a body is defined not by its shape and appearance but by its capacities: what it can feel and do, how it connects with other bodies. From this angle one could say: shame about the body looks at it as a picture to be compared with a model. But the body is not a picture; it is a power. It dances, hugs, walks, gets tired and recovers. Ask not “what does it look like?” but “what is it capable of?” — the answer may surprise you.
body_shame.practice: List five things your body managed to do today. Not how it looked — what it did.

quote.text: …no one has yet determined what the body can do.
quote.author: Baruch Spinoza (one of Deleuze's favorite formulas)

illness.text: Illness is hard: the body lets you down, and familiar life changes. Your feelings — fear, anger, fatigue — are legitimate. Deleuze himself lived for many years with a serious lung disease and went on thinking and writing; he admitted that his fragile health in its own way sharpened his sense of life. In The Logic of Sense he cites the words of the poet Joë Bousquet, confined to bed after being wounded in the war. Deleuze saw in them not submission but a way of making what happened one's own, of finding in it a sense one had not chosen. From this angle one could say: illness is not the whole of your life, but something with which you can build a relationship, not only fight.
illness.practice: Write down what you noticed today — a sound, light, a taste — that you wouldn't have noticed at your usual pace.

quote.text: My wound existed before me, I was born to embody it.
quote.author: Joë Bousquet (quoted by Deleuze)
quote.source: Deleuze, The Logic of Sense (1969), Twenty-First Series of the Event

pride.text: Pride in what you have done is a good, legitimate feeling. Spinoza called the joy that arises when a person sees their own power of acting “self-contentment,” and Deleuze, following him, valued such joys: you did something and saw what you are capable of. In his book on Nietzsche, Deleuze distinguished active and reactive forces. Reactive pride compares: “I'm better than them.” Active pride affirms: “I did this, and it is good.” From this angle one could say: healthy pride is an affect of affirmation, a joy in your own strength that needs no one else's defeat. There's no need to hide it. Allow yourself to be glad — and notice what new steps it opens up.
pride.practice: Say one sentence of affirmation out loud to yourself: “I did this, and it is good.” No comparisons.

melancholy.text: Gentle sadness is a subtle feeling in which sorrow and tenderness are intertwined. Deleuze and Guattari wrote about the “refrain” — a little tune, a motif that keeps coming back. They believed that music takes such tunes — lullabies, children's songs, songs about home — and carries them further, turning the familiar into something new and open. From this angle one could say: melancholy is like a refrain. It brings back something old and dear and at the same time gently lets it go, turning it into a melody. It doesn't need fixing. It is an affect in which the past doesn't hold you but sounds. You can simply listen to it, the way you listen to a favorite, slightly sad piece of music.
melancholy.practice: Hum or play the melody that is sounding in you right now. Listen to it to the end, without changing anything.
